<reason>Side B won the decisive clashes. First, on overbreadth: A's attempted rescue of security tools via "activation is the opt-in" and "the motion does cover it—and should" for bank fraud models handed B two concessions B exploited precisely—activation-as-consent guts the motion's protection, and signup consent is exactly the "checkbox theater" A disowned. Second, on multi-party consent: A's fork (capture opt-in or de-identify at ingestion) was creative, but B showed the non-consent branch is B's own engineering remedy, and A never repaired the contradiction that the phisher/scammer party to a communication cannot be consented for under A's own [A1.3] rule. Third, A's unlearning pressure question was handled honestly by B ("I won't fake one") and then turned: A's own ingestion-fallback showed the harm is preventable upstream. A's closing offered a decent prevention-versus-repair distinction and a partial answer on adversaries, but it was clipped and did not resolve the checkbox contradiction. B's speeches consistently narrowed the dispute and forced A into reading exceptions into the motion as written; A's later speeches relied increasingly on redefinitions B flagged in real time.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 [B4.1-B4.8] was the decisive exchange: it tallied A's live concessions—the admitted coverage of bank fraud models, the "activation is the opt-in" redefinition, and A's adoption of de-identification at ingestion as B's own remedy—then added the adversary-consent point (phishers never opt in) and the organ-donation defaults point to answer A's Q2, converting A's pressure questions into B's material.</best_rebuttal>
